rationale: A wins because it knows where the floorboards are weak and names them before a reporter does. Its best line, "The '70% lower than cards' claim — where account-to-account actually beats interchange," turns Plaid's own asterisk into the story. B has useful shapes, but "Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before" imports an unsourced history lesson and then builds an angle on it. That is how a smart draft talks itself into a fact-check problem.
gaps_in_A: "FedNow gets its first big merchant-payments use case" overclaims. The update says Pay by Bank uses FedNow rails; it does not prove first, big, production volume, or merchant adoption.
"a 12,000-institution connector is now positioned as a card-network bypass" is defensible, but it risks blurring Plaid's total institution coverage with actual Pay by Bank/FedNow availability.
The first and third angles slightly crowd each other: both lean on alternative rails challenging cards; the FedNow angle needs independent adoption context to stand alone.
gaps_in_B: "Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before" is not in the update. It may be a good skeptical angle, but presented this way it is an invented premise wearing a columnist's jacket.

"instant-settlement rail" and "settlement-speed problem" go beyond the facts. The update says instant bank verification and FedNow rails; it does not say prior failures were caused by settlement speed.
"furniture, travel, auto, B2B invoicing" are plausible high-ticket examples, but they are not supplied merchant verticals. Useful brainstorm, bad as grounded angle copy.
"FedNow policy/infrastructure-adoption angle ... duplicate" throws away a potentially distinct rail-adoption story too quickly; A handles that altitude better.
